title: High yield synthesis of type-II red phosphorus crystals
content: Type-II red phosphorus represents the first elemental phosphorus allotrope composed of regularly arranged helical wavy monochiral tubes. Compared to fibrous phosphorus, black phosphorus, and violet phosphorus, it exhibits more pronounced crystal orientation-dependent optical responses, emerging as a promising low-dimensional semiconductor material for polarization-sensitive optoelectronic devices. The synthesis of high-quality type-II red phosphorus is crucial for both experimental investigation and practical applications. However, since its initial report in 1947, crystal preparation has remained challenging, confining related research to preliminary structural characterization until recent success in growing single crystals and determining its crystal structure. Achieving high-yield synthesis of highly crystalline type-II red phosphorus has become imperative for advancing research on this material. In this study, the efficient and controlled synthesis of type-II red phosphorus was achieved through systematic optimization of the synergistic conditions of multiple parameters during the chemical vapour transport process. Initially, tin (Sn) was identified as the optimal mineralizing agent based on theoretical calculations and experimental results. Further, precise thermal control strategies were formulated in conjunction with thermogravimetric analysis to effectively regulate the yield of the product. Moreover, the duration of each reaction stage was adjusted to elucidate the kinetic growth pathways of the crystals, improving both crystallization quality and synthesis efficiency. Building thereon, the nucleation mechanism of type-II red phosphorus was further elucidated, confirming that type-V phosphorus forms preferentially at the nucleation centre whilst type-II phosphorus grows in its periphery, thereby confirming the existence of competitive nucleation. Consequently, type-II red phosphorus crystals with high crystallinity and a yield as high as 97.6% were obtained in just three days. The findings lay a material foundation for its applications in electronics, photonics and catalysis, whilst providing a generalisable strategy for the controlled synthesis of metastable phosphorus allotropes.
